https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.subtitle: Jennifer Kowalski and Cole Macdonald deny causing at least £52,000 of damage
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.text:
Two Just Stop Oil (JSO) activists have denied causing at least £52,000 of damage after two private jets were sprayed with orange paint at Stansted.
Jennifer Kowalski, 28, of Dumbarton in Scotland, and Cole Macdonald, 22, of Brighton, pleaded not guilty to causing criminal damage and interfering with national infrastructure at Chelmsford crown court.
The pair are alleged to have used angle grinders to break through an airport fence at around 5am on July 20 before entering a taxiway with Just Stop Oil-branded fire extinguishers filled with orange spray paint.
The prosecution said that cleaning up the paint cost £52,000, although the extent of the damage to the fence and the cost of extra security in the aftermath was not yet known.
The court heard that thousands of passengers were affected because 75 flights were disrupted during a 38-minute delay.
Kowalski and Macdonald previously denied causing criminal damage and interfering with national infrastructure at an earlier appearance at Chelmsford magistrates’ court. They were also charged with aggravated trespass, though they had not been asked to enter pleas until now.
At the time of the incident, Essex police said it detained two people who gained access to a private area of an airfield and were “causing damage to two aircraft”.
The aircraft were owned by Prudential Insurance and by an investment group, according to charges read to the court.
The two defendants are due to stand for a four-day trial at the same court from September 15 next year.
Judge Mary Loram KC granted both defendants bail, with conditions including that they do not go within a mile of an airport apart from on moving public transport.
The force confirmed that the private jet of Taylor Swift, which JSO said had landed at Stansted “mere hours before”, was not at the airport.

https://www.thetimes.com/comment/columni.title: Riots teach us about public order, not migrants
https://www.thetimes.com/comment/columni.text:
I first heard about Stacey Vint’s fall as she pushed a burning wheelie bin at a police cordon while someone online was explaining to me how the social disorder that followed the Southport stabbings should be interpreted as a serious contribution to our national debate on immigration.
I’ve forgotten now which variety of comment this was. I was in receipt of two kinds. From the right, drunk people throwing bricks were the inevitable consequence of the political failings of the metropolitan elite. From the left, the cause (and I did have one person seriously advance this) of Stacey’s bin fiasco, or of an 18-year-old who had failed to take his ADHD medication before smashing the window of a police Ford Focus, was right-wing rhetoric such as Theresa May’s “citizens of nowhere” speech.
Well, I may be wrong, but I think Stacey might have missed the then prime minister’s 2016 conference address. And I don’t think Declan Geiran, with his long history of burglary, criminal damage, supplying Class A drugs and failing to follow court orders, set fire to a police transit van in order to register a point about how the refugee convention is being interpreted by the British asylum system.
I simply refuse to treat these thuggish acts of violence as if they were some sort of debating point in the immigration argument. This is partly on principle. In so far as any of these criminals had anything useful to say, I absolutely will not acknowledge a political point made that way, and I don’t think anyone else should either.
But it is partly because of my observations of the events themselves and the people involved. I do not believe this was a mass political protest giving expression to frustration about immigration policy. Nor do I think it was because of media and political discourse about race. Instead it was a combination of organised disruption by a small but vicious far-right clique, who have a niche political view they were trying to advance, and drink and drug-fuelled summer violence.
This, it is important to emphasise, is not to suggest that both racism and immigration policy are unworthy of intense discussion and constructive action. But these violent incidents are not any sort of contribution to either.
Nor am I am suggesting the sometimes buffoonish nature of the criminality means these events shouldn’t be taken seriously. The whole thing must have been incredibly frightening for all ethnic minorities and, in particular, the Muslim community. It might take them a long time to regain a feeling of security. And the violence against the police was unconscionable. So it was a social disaster.
It is just that I think the primary lessons to be learnt are ones about law and order rather than migration.
First, the episode reinforces the arguments of those of us who insist our political disputes must never be settled on the streets. Of course there must always be the right in a free society to protest. But this is only one right and has to be balanced against other rights. Which includes the right to go about one’s normal business safely and expeditiously.
There are many ways of making your point in a free society and it is quite possible to change the law using elections and political dialogue. It is unnecessary to attempt such change by large demonstrations of physical support for a cause or by obstructing other people. That doesn’t mean such activity should be banned. But it does mean there need to be laws that put some limits on the nuisance to others and allow the police to act with confidence and speed.
The frightening, crude and bigoted behaviour of the far-right clique makes this point eloquently. And perhaps now it might be better understood by those who resisted it when the demonstrators were making points about climate change they approved of.
Laws governing the right to protest are not — as these incidents make clear — attacks on a liberal society. They are an attempt to balance rights and encourage people to make political points through the political system — the greatest possible protection of a liberal society.
This is also why the tough sentences given to Just Stop Oil motorway protesters were justified. If it is fine to try to change energy policy by dangerous acts of disruption, why not immigration policy? Or policy on abortion? I think the previous government’s moves to restrict such activity were right. And I suspect Keir Starmer won’t repeal them.
The other law and order lesson from the recent violent outbursts is that deterrence appears to work. Something that seems common sense, but is often doubted. I’m sure there will be careful studies, but it does look as though further violence was, in part, prevented by the imposition of lengthy prison sentences for early offenders.
There is an important qualification to add. The deterrence worked because justice was speedy. There was a connection made between the crime and the consequences of the crime. And often, there simply isn’t.
The last government left the court system in disrepair. The backlog is huge (there are almost 70,000 trials outstanding at crown courts) and cases can often take more than a year to get to court, even after the time taken to decide about charges. The average waiting time between being charged and the case completing in the crown courts is about 300 days.
This isn’t fair on victims, on defendants, or on those working in the criminal law, who are (still, despite the recent dispute) underpaid and working in crumbling courts. What the race violence demonstrates is that it is not fair on the rest of us either. Because a slow courts system undermines deterrence.
Quite a lot of the crimes for which the race demonstrators were convicted were impetuous and committed under the influence of drink and drugs. A fair number of them seemed to have only a hazy recollection of their crime even the next day. Try them in a year’s time and much of the link between their sentences and their behaviour will have gone, both for them and for the rest of us.
What is true for them is true more widely. A faster justice system is better for fighting crime. The last government was so busy laughing at lefty lawyers from Islington it overlooked the fact that what they’ve been saying on the court system is right.
This is not to suggest all criminal cases should be prosecuted and completed within a couple of days in order to make the evening news. This isn’t possible or even desirable. But I do think, alongside insisting that laws be made through peaceful engagement, that ensuring justice be swiftly and fairly administered is a vital part of a stable liberal order.
If Stacey and her wobbly wheelie bin is going to teach us anything, let it be that.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.title: Jess Phillips: ‘People think MPs are useless, posh and corrupt’
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.text:
As I’m on the train to Birmingham to talk to Jess Phillips, she’s trending on X/Twitter. This isn’t a rare occurrence, it has to be said. Other MPs smoothed their way to Westminster via Oxbridge, and then business, PR or the City — learning to be blandly but firmly noncommittal along the way.
Phillips came via the Women’s Aid Federation, working with abused women in Sandwell in the West Midlands, and her “no-nonsense Auntie Jess in the pub just saying it like it is” vibe has consistently made her a regular “incident” on the world’s tetchiest social media platform. Her use of metaphor when talking about Jeremy Corbyn (“I won’t knife you in the back, I’ll knife you in the front”); her brisk disagreements with Diane Abbott (whom she told to “f*** off”).
Today’s X, however, is both particularly furious and particularly badly spelt about her.
“Your [sic] a disgrace.” “We need Jess Phillips sacked and locked up for excinciting violence.” “My advice is SHUT UP.” “You will do anything for votes, sucking up Jess we see you.” “She doesnt care, she’s a wronging [sic].” “Horrible dish [sic] wife.”
The night before we meet, following days of rioting, there were social media rumours of another far-right protest in Birmingham. A gang of roughly 200 Asian men turned up to the location — and met no far-right rioters. Self-commissioning some “freelance violence”, about 50 of them then surrounded a local pub and beat up a young white man — all of which was captured on dozens of iPhones and then broadcast on the news.
Phillips, watching her constituency explode, tweeted, “These people came to this location because it has been spread that racists were coming to attack them. This misinformation was spread entirely to create this content.”
Since the post, Phillips has been trending constantly. She’s accused of “making excuses” for the Muslim community; of “pandering”; of “being scared” of her Muslim constituents. The cries for her to “be SACKED!” are constant.
• Jess Phillips: why I resigned, what Keir said, and my breast op
It’s quite the day to visit the new parliamentary under-secretary of state for safeguarding and violence against women and girls.
I ring on her doorbell. She answers.
“Hello!” she says. She’s in a stripy top and jeans. Barefoot. “Sorry — I thought you were coming at 12pm? I’m in a meeting with the Home Office. Do you want to sit in the kitchen?”
I check my phone. My appointment was, indeed, at 12pm.
After apologising, I kill some time by wandering through her neighbourhood. For an area that’s been in the news for violent rioting and racial unrest — one friend’s mother texted me to ask if it was “safe” to travel through Birmingham today on a train — it’s very peaceful. The HQ of Moseley Folk Festival has a mural on the side of Radio 1 DJ Janice Long saying, “Hello you!” An elderly Asian man is watering his hydrangeas. There’s a garden reclamation yard where I wonder if I want to buy an old Victorian hay cart or not.
Eventually I loop back to Phillips’s house. For those who wonder what kind of lifestyle MPs have, Phillips’s house is a Victorian terrace, with a massive TV in the bay window, but it is also — and I hope Phillips won’t mind me saying this — by far the scruffiest on the street. Given how high profile and controversial Phillips is, I wonder if anyone could guess this is her house. In the main, I conclude not — but there is a massive gold hoop earring on the doorstep, which might tip people off. Phillips is known for her earrings.
At 12pm, I ring the doorbell again. There is a pause, and then a teenage boy with wet hair, and wearing sunglasses, answers it.
“I’m here to see your mum,” I say.
He nods, shows me into the kitchen, and then wanders off. When Phillips finally joins me, in the garden, she’s cheerful, but clearly tired.
“You’re trending again,” I say, sympathetically.
“Oh, always,” Phillips says, getting out a vape the size of a clarinet. “When you trend and it’s just ‘Jess’, though — not even ‘Jess Phillips’ — it does make you feel like, I dunno, Madonna.”
• Domestic homicide reviews are pointless, says Jess Phillips
We sit for a minute. Phillips exhales her vape. She looks across the lawn.
“The slugs have mullered those hostas,” she says.
“So — on the phone to the Home Office. Are you in trouble?” I ask. “Have all those tweets saying you should be sacked worked?”
“No!” Phillips snorts. “They can all save their time. Don’t worry. I don’t need to trend on Twitter. I’m perfectly capable of getting myself fired all by myself.”
“Did you get, then, like, a bollocking?”
“To be honest, they’ve never given me a massive bollocking.” As Phillips says this, she sounds surprised herself. “In years gone by, I’ve had whips saying, ‘Just take it down. It’s going to cause grief for us,’ because I’m a bit sweary, aren’t I? But they don’t tend to mind [swearing]. Yes, I have a different job now, but yesterday I was just tweeting as an angry resident of Birmingham Yardley, not as a government minister. I wish I hadn’t bothered, because it’s all pointless.”
Phillips explains what happened. She was coming back “from a book talk, in Bath” on the train, when she heard what was occurring.
The first thing to do was call the police. “Obviously, when I say ‘call the police’, I don’t call the police. I just text the chief constable. He’s a lovely guy, my chief constable. Very responsive.”
All the previously gathered intelligence on the planned far-right “protests” — with a list of more than 100 locations, circulated on social media — was that it was a hoax. “It’s a way to get a load of angry people [Muslims] on the streets. It’s so obvious when people are being puppeteered.”
Eager to stop Muslim counterprotests, Phillips had spent the day on the phone to various community leaders — “people in mosques, people in the constituency” — giving “a whole lot of reassurance” and trying to get them to be the “message-carriers”. “Hours and hours of effort,” she says. “People say, ‘No one was trying to prevent it.’ ‘The police didn’t turn up.’ Of course we were trying to prevent it! Of course the police turned up! But when you’ve got loads of people on the streets, they get delayed.
“This is why I [went on X] and was like, ‘I just want people to know the truth: this is what’s been happening all day.’ ” (She has since described her tweet as a “mistake”, saying, “I think I almost certainly could have phrased it better.”)
The irony, of course, is that Phillips is trending on X as someone who is trying to “appease Muslims”; as someone who is “scared” of her Muslim constituents; who is their “handmaiden”, when just a month ago — “It’s a month today. F***ing hell. It feels like a year” — one of the most notable moments on election night was Phillips’s count being disrupted by pro-Gaza Muslim protests.
Over cries of “shame on you” and “free Gaza”, Phillips’s victory was finally announced — her 10,659 majority cut to just 693 — and when she gave her speech, she often had to shout to be heard.
“I see we’re going to continue with the class we had during the campaign,” she started, looking, frankly, furious. “I will carry on with my speech. I understand that a strong woman standing up to you is met with such reticence.”
Phillips had been screamed at in the street; was filmed everywhere she went. One of her campaigners had her car tyres slashed.
“This is the worst election I have ever stood in,” she said at the time.
• Labour MPs hit out at intimidation as Gaza revolt rocks party
Phillips has recently returned from giving evidence in a court case against those involved.
So half of Phillips’s critics think she “panders” to Muslims; the other half are “a small minority” of Muslims who think she’s anti-Muslim. It sounds like… she’s a centrist?
“You know what? I’m just Birmingham,” Phillips says. “I’m fair to everyone. I think all awful, angry men — and it’s always men — using various issues as an excuse to be violent should go to jail. Do you know what happened when I rang the woman who runs the pub [the Clumsy Swan, in Yardley] where the attack happened? I was ringing to make sure if she was OK, if she needed any help, if she needed me to get involved. And she was more concerned about a woman in her car park who’d lost her shoe.”
And to be fair — and “to be fair” is the primary catchphrase of those from the Midlands — this is a very Birmingham attitude. Focus on the immediate problem, keep a downbeat sense of humour, and always go after a missing shoe. You don’t want to ruin a good pair.
“Focusing on the immediate problem” is very much Jess Phillips’s strength. In her hugely entertaining new book, Let’s Be Honest, Phillips is very good at explaining how the MPs that you see on the news, asking provocative questions in Westminster or engaging in “culture war” rhetoric are — and here she is brisk — “complete dickheads”.
“I guess if you’ve never changed a single law, never made a decent speech, never been called on for your in-depth knowledge on a particular policy area, then that is the only way to make your mark on modern politics,” she says, as someone who has regularly done all three.
She then gives the example of Nick Fletcher — who lost his seat in the last election — making a widely reported comment on how men and boys were losing fictional role models, since there was an all-female reboot of Ghostbusters. “Is there any wonder we are seeing so many young men committing crime?” Fletcher asked, before suggesting there be a minister for men.
“I don’t mind what Nick Fletcher is saying; I don’t disagree that men need good role models on telly,” Phillips writes. “But what efforts has [Fletcher] made to set up youth services in his constituency? Where are the debates where he’s joined with mental health campaigners… to stem the tide of young men dying by suicide? If you want a minister for men, come on, Nick — convene with a group of experts, meet with groups of affected men, and put pen to paper. That’s what I do when I want something that doesn’t exist. And eventually, the government gives in — because I’m a pain in the arse.”
• Who wants a minister for men? Here’s their brief
“You know what?” Phillips says today.“I hate that loads of people think MPs are generally posh, useless, rich, corrupt individuals doing nothing. Because, truly, most of the MPs I know are really hard-working and totally normal. We all use the NHS and the buses. After a vote, you see everyone just getting on the Tube home. We all buy, you know, bin bags. And these people really care. But there are some people who just don’t see the difference between talking about something, and getting on the telly, and actually doing something. And it’s not just in politics. We live in a social media age, don’t we? It’s all about being seen to be angry.”
This reminds me of an anecdote Phillips once told me, which I beg her to tell again today. About Extinction Rebellion.
“Oh God, yes.”
A few years ago, some campaigners from Extinction Rebellion contacted Phillips, to support their cause.
“And I should add here, none of them were from Yardley. I’ve had not one letter about Extinction Rebellion from my constituents. Most of them either work at the airport or in car manufacture. Fossil fuel industries.”
Nonetheless, in the spirit of saving the planet, Phillips took the meeting. The campaigners came into the office — and immediately sat on the floor.
“I think they thought chairs were hierarchical,” she says.
Additionally, when someone said something the campaigners agreed with, they didn’t say anything, or clap. “They just silently did ‘jazz hands’. It was quite spooky.”
Phillips — “Sitting on a chair. I don’t want to waste a chair” — asked how she could help. The campaigners seemed confused. Phillips explained that she needed specific policy ideas from them — actual issues she could help with.
“I tried to help them. I was like, ‘How about packaging? Excess supermarket packaging? I think most people are annoyed by that — that’s something that would engage my constituents. Or retro-fitting their damp houses with insulation?’ I was just riffing, off the top of my head. To help them.”
The Extinction campaigners — “one of whom genuinely was called Tarquin” — seemed nonplussed at these small offers.
“They just wanted me to say, ‘OK, I’ll write a law called ‘Totally Saving the World’. Thanks for popping by, guys. You reminded me,’ ” Phillips says. “They just thought you complain to a politician and then we sort it all out. And that’s not how it works. We have to be given specific ideas we can help with. And I think we all know that when we’re younger. I’ll get kids writing to me about litter in their local area and I’ll say, ‘What do you think you could do?’ And they come up with answers, and then I suggest ways I can help, and they get it! It just seems you get to a certain age and think… being on social media shouting about it is better than actually coming up with solutions.”
“Coming up with solutions” is now, finally, after the landslide Labour win, within Phillips’s power. In reviews of Let’s Be Honest, some critics affected polite distaste at her bold claim to be “the best at my job” — but it’s hard to think of anyone else who has worked so long, and so effectively, to raise the profile of violence against women and girls. It was Phillips who worked with campaigners to collate the first yearly list of women who had been killed by men — her reading out their names in parliament, to hushed horror, has now become a sad annual ritual. As she is now parliamentary under-secretary of state for safeguarding and violence against women and girls, how quickly will we see change?
“We’re going to have to be honest how slow it will be,” Phillips says, sombrely. “This year, women are still going to die at exactly the same rate as they did last year.”
When we talk about male violence against women and girls, what are we talking about? Presumably the majority of men are good, decent people who are horrified by it?
“It’s 1 in 20,” Phillips says, immediately. “Two weeks ago the NPCC [National Police Chiefs’ Council] came up with this figure. One in twenty men is involved in violence against women and children. Which is quite a lot. Yeah. And the largest growing cohort is 16-25. These are very, very young men being violent to women.”
So — without being Extinction Rebellion, sitting on the floor, doing silent jazz hands — what causes male violence, Jess Phillips? Do you have all the answers?
“Not being in control of what boys see is a problem,” Phillips says. “I’m not saying we need total control over their social media. I spent five minutes on my sons’ WhatsApp before finding it so inane I thought, ‘If they are being groomed by terrorists, I can’t even be bothered with it. It’s so boring.’ But the prevailing wind — porn, women being groomed as sex objects — they need to have the critical thinking space to get a balanced view. To be truthful, we don’t yet know what will work. We’re going to have to invest in finding out, aren’t we? And it’s going to take a long time.”
Presumably the sons of superfeminist Jess Phillips aren’t violent misogynists. How have you, personally, prevented that?
“Well, when they’ve had kids at school saying, ‘Feminism’s gone too far,’ they’re immediately like, ‘Don’t be ridiculous. How can it? Women haven’t even got equality yet.’ Porn? We’re brutal with it. We tell them, ‘Nobody in real life chokes each other.’ And so my kids have a next-level lack of embarrassment about sex. I vividly remember Danny asking my mother-in-law, at dinner, if she’d masturbated. She spat out her tea, laughing. He was seven. And he said, ‘There’s no shame in it, Nanny.’ ”
Phillips hoots at the memory.
“And their dad, Tom — if they’re asserting something about women, Tom will say, very fiercely, ‘You get to have an opinion on this, but ultimately, your mother’s opinion overrides it, because she lives it. You can’t say what it’s like for a woman.’ Before now, they’ve told me my lipstick is for ‘the male gaze’. I was like, ‘F*** off. It’s actually to impress other women, you eejit.’ ”
Tom, Phillips’s husband, is here. He’d earlier come into the garden and surprised her.
“What are you doing here?” she asked.
“It’s dinner time. I’ve come home for my dinner,” he said.
“Do you always do that?” she asked, before turning to me and saying, “I don’t know, do I? I’m never here. No idea what he’s usually doing.”
Tom is a strapping, beardy former builder, with a very dry sense of humour. On hearing Phillips’s reply, I have to say, I have a moment of profound longing. If only there were more beardy alphas telling young men their mothers’ opinions on women “overrode” theirs, I can’t help but think the world would be a better place.
“The good thing is, there’s already loads of legislation in place that would improve things,” Phillips says, businesslike, refilling her vape. “We just don’t use it. It is illegal to rape — although you wouldn’t know it from the conviction rates. The conversation about making violence against women equal to terrorism? It doesn’t matter how many times people say it — so far, practically, it’s being treated like it’s not. But I can tell you right now it’s not the civil service or the police [slowing things down.] It’s the politicians. It’s top-down. Will is the most important thing. It outstrips any currency. And the ultimate person this all rides on is the prime minister — and Keir Starmer really gives a toss about violence against women and girls. I feel like No 10 is breathing down my neck on this. It’s pretty fierce.”
It’s nearly time for me to go — Phillips has told me she has to “be out at three”. I presume it’s another Home Office Zoom. “No, I’m meeting a mate in the pub,” she says, cackling.
As we finish our tea, we go back to talking about that febrile election night, just four weeks ago. How Phillips had intended to bring the family of the late MP Jo Cox, who was murdered in 2016, to the count but couldn’t, as the atmosphere was so violent.
“Brendan Cox [Jo’s widower], he’s now married to Anna, who works in my constituency, and she’s pregnant. And the idea that something might happen to her around an election and it’s somehow my fault…” Phillips shudders. “Or my kids, seeing their mum…”
Words, for the first time today, fail her.
You seem to feel shame, I say. Guilt. Like, your job makes you a liability to them.
“Yes! I am a liability to them. Their safety. Because of this job. You know,” she muses, “I thought about this, and if I had lost that night, in many ways my life would be so much easier. I’d know my husband comes home from work at dinner time. I’d have more time off. And I’d earn way more money. Doing all that media stuff? [Phillips has written four books, and presented Have I Got News for You.] No offence, but it’s easy. And I’d definitely be safer. We’d all be safer. I have security now. I can’t drive my car any more. We had so many threats — that they’d do something to my car…” She pauses. “Blowing it up?”
Phillips tries to say this casually. But, in the event, it’s impossible to talk casually about people blowing up your family’s car.
“I just want to say, in my normal life, I feel perfectly safe,” Phillips says, trying to be cheerful. “When I’m not working, I’ll walk home from my friends’ house, pissed, at midnight. And I’ve got amazing family and friends, who understand it all.
“Here, this is funny,” she says, getting out her phone. “You know how, on election night, it was too close to call? No one knew if I’d lost or not — not the news, not the counters, not the party, no one. You know who did know? Joe Lycett.”
She shows me her phone.
“Joe Lycett, texting me at 3am, going, ‘Well done, bab.’ He saw some bloke called Neil on the internet call it — that it was by 600 votes and everything. How the f***k did Neil on the internet, and then Joe Lycett, know, when f***ing Sky News didn’t? And then he texted, ‘Forever amazed by your bravery.’ Hahaha!”
Phillips hoots again, as if this is another wry joke by Joe Lycett.

https://www.thetimes.com/comment/the-tim.title: The Times view on riots: Instigators
https://www.thetimes.com/comment/the-tim.text:
The riots that blighted Britain’s towns and cities throughout the weekend are an utter disgrace. Scores of police have been injured, some seriously. Shops have been looted and burnt, property vandalised, mosques besieged and Muslims intimidated. Mindless violence has lured bored young thugs into city centres with little aim and no discernible agenda except to shout abuse, smash buildings and assault anyone the far right sees as a target for its racist intolerance. The government, rightly, has demanded a fast and tough response. All those arrested are likely to be charged. Courts must hand out exemplary sentences.
The rioters’ agenda may be mindless. But the way they are contacted, organised, incited and let loose on cities is far from mindless. Social media have become the hate-mongers directing inchoate anger and frustration against targets that the so-called English Defence League and other ­extremists, largely — but not only — on the far right see as enemies of their white, nationalist cause. Millions of people hourly check the latest posts on TikTok, Instagram, Telegram, Twitter/X and those other platforms that appear to dominate the thinking and actions of the gullible and the malign. It is a clear danger to social cohesion. It is also a disgraceful refusal by very rich social media providers to take responsibility for the disinformation that they allow — to their huge financial profit — to be posted on their platforms.
The Online Safety Act, passed last year after years of frustrating debate and legal squabbling, was intended to shield young people from violent pornography by insisting on age verification. It ­also required digital media companies to restrict children’s access to material promoting suicide, self-harm or eating disorders — although material considered “legal but harmful” was not, after arguments over definition, banned outright. This is clearly inadequate.
In an interview with The Times today, Deputy Chief Constable Maggie Blyth said big technology companies were still ­“fuelling” violence by allowing aggressive, misogyn­istic content on their social media platforms and failing to curb incendiary posts.
Equally worryingly, social media platforms are now the means of choice for those intent on sowing disinformation, fomenting social unrest and spreading hate and prejudice — the modern equivalent of Der Stürmer in Nazi Germany. Russia has armies of malign online propagandists ready to hack into western media and post mendacious information designed to incite hatred, sow confusion and deepen divisions in western societies. Little attempt has been made to trace and block this poison. Social media companies have been warned repeatedly by western intelligence agencies and have turned a blind eye.
Ofcom is now considering how to make the legislation more robust. This is urgent. The Online Safety Act must be broadened to stop the huge rise in incitement to violence, disorder, rioting and social harm. The far right now campaigns largely, and alarmingly successfully, on social ­media. So too do causes at the other end of the spectrum, including extremists such as Just Stop Oil, purportedly campaigning to limit climate change. Their incitements to block motorways and cause civil damage have rightly been answered with prison sentences for the instigators.
Champions of civil liberty claim to be alarmed by any clampdown on digital media as a limit on freedom of expression. This is naive self-deception. It ignores the ruthless use of algorithms by profitable platforms that are pushing addictive content on the unwary. It ignores the huge social and material costs of the rioting and destruction instigated by social media posts. The Online Safety Act was primarily aimed to safeguard children. It must now be revised to ensure that it guards the safety and security of all society.

https://www.thetimes.com/comment/columni.title: Keir Starmer must look beyond the riot sanctions
https://www.thetimes.com/comment/columni.text:
A line from the American broadcaster Fred Rogers springs welcomingly to memory. “When I was a boy and would see scary things in the news, my mother would say to me, ‘Look for the helpers. You will always find people who are helping.’”
Last week we saw the dance teacher who defended the Southport children, the neighbours who ran to help, the community that brought brushes and shovels after the riot and rebuilt the mosque wall. We saw Muslim, Jewish and Christian religious leaders processing quietly together to say “Hate will not prevail”. In the first Liverpool riot, help came from counterprotesters standing to defend the mosque, an elderly lady brandishing her banner “Nans against Nazis” and hundreds singing “There are many, many more of us than you” to the tune of Comin’ Round the Mountain.
Many, many more. We need to remember that most people are not malicious, or opportunist vandals, or even victims of the dim, unreflective stupidity that gets swayed by online lies. Most people also understand that although no force is perfect, the police are not oppressors but ourselves in uniform: a vital organ of society. They are pledged defenders of safety and democracy, and to injure and insult them is self-harm.
So there was some comfort in “looking for the helpers”, and including the stretched, battered police force in that. But there is anger too, a punitive instinct demanding redress. One much-repeated clip online was of a Southport rioter in a grey tracksuit who was taunting the police cordon before being struck on the head with a missile poorly aimed by a comrade. As he staggered away he got another brick in the groin. Hard not to cheer.
A day later Hartlepool offered a similar small consolation: a man confronting the police bitten on the bum by a police dog, his shorts half pulled off. In court later that same man snivelled tearfully, murmuring: “Thank you, judge, thank you.”
That court scene mattered. The rapid serves-him-right moment in an online clip briefly relieves outrage, but instant karma is not enough and the new prime minister’s first response demonstrated an important facet of his leadership. Sir Keir Starmer was director of public prosecutions in 2011, another hot summer of trouble. His reaction as a public official was to speed up prosecution, running night and weekend courts (which some defence lawyers felt led to conveyor-belt justice) and generally demonstrating to perpetrators that joining a ruck brought you only trouble.
He has done the same now, rapidly convening police chiefs and ministers with instructions about speed: 90 new prosecutors as I write. Interestingly, a year after those 2011 riots Starmer said he believed that the speed was a more effective deterrent than heavy sentences: if people saw their companions in court 24 or 48 hours later, they’d think again.
There are big differences today. For one thing the justice system is in a far worse state: the court backlog continues to rise, up 8 per cent over the past year, even after the end of the pandemic. Half our magistrates’ courts were closed between 2010 and 2018. Police numbers have only just returned to 2010 strength after a long dip, which has to suggest that there are fewer experienced officers around to lead others through a crisis like this. We are getting bored with the new government’s constant harping at the mess the Tories left, but face it, the figures do tell a story.
Another big difference is that research on the 2011 riots by the London School of Economics showed that two thirds were in London, the principal charge was for looting and half the perpetrators were under 20. Only 6 per cent were over 40. Today’s TV footage and early court reports suggest a different profile: mid-life, often employed, fathers. Grown men who should be steady but whose discontent and credulity were easily stirred into rage at an establishment they think privileges a foe.
The prime minister’s first response was solid in character: meet destructive rage with prompt justice. He is no rhetorician and there’s unshowy solidity in his flat “I will not permit, under any circumstances, a breakdown in law and order on our streets”. But as days and months go by we will need more. In a practical sense perhaps more inventive deterrence, since short jail sentences are famously not educative or useful, and prisons are full.
Think tags, severe curfews, rigorous and visibly shaming community penalties. Perhaps a period’s confiscation of passport: no football matches abroad, no family holiday, no stag sprees. Many — including citizens badly disrupted by Just Stop Oil or Black Lives Matter — would also welcome a ban on disguising face coverings around public buildings: France, the Netherlands and Switzerland have introduced that.
But in a wider sense we need distinctive leadership, a sense of steady mission beyond the merely economic (although the geography of protest certainly makes northern levelling up a priority). Open and even-handed justice must defy the nervous shibboleths that helped the spreaders of racist disinformation, such as the anxiety about upsetting “communities”.
Immigration management is obviously vital. The demographic make-up of the new government should also, in time, reduce the widespread belief that the white working-class majority are despised and will get more roughly treated than minorities, their comfortable liberal spokesmen and luxury-believers who block roads. Leadership should also express a healthy, optimistic patriotism to counteract the darker variety of the English Defence League.
Conveying this message may be harder for the lawyerly Starmer than his well-rehearsed judicial crackdown. But it matters. In the coming months we will find out what sort of prime minister we have.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.title: Judge tells JSO: Easy to be blasé when it’s not your life disrupted
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.subtitle: Five Just Stop Oil members have been jailed for causing gridlock on the M25. A sixth protester was handed a suspended prison sentence
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.text:
Five Just Stop Oil activists who conspired to cause gridlock on the M25 have been jailed by a judge, who told them it was easy to be dismissive when it was “not your life that’s being disrupted”.
George Simonson and Theresa Higginson were each sentenced to two years, Paul Bell was sentenced to 22 months, and Gaie Delap and Paul Sousek were sentenced to 20 months for their part in the protests in November 2022.
A sixth defendant, Daniel Johnson, was given a 21-month sentence suspended for two years and ordered to complete 200 hours of community service.
The five, aged 24 to 77, had pleaded guilty at an earlier hearing to causing a public nuisance after they caused mass disruption by climbing gantries on the M25 on November 9, 2022.
Sentencing the activists at Basildon crown court, Judge Shane Collery KC said: “It’s easy to be blasé and dismissive when it’s not your life that’s being disrupted. He added: “Many people suffered hours of delay [and] your actions were disproportionate to your aims.”
The judge noted that an accident had happened near one gantry and it was “fortunate more accidents did not occur”.
He said their purpose was to “create mass disruption so Just Stop Oil would benefit from the media interest it would create”, and described the protest as “perhaps a curious way of seeking to influence the public opinion”.
Collery told them: “[You] considered you knew better than everyone else”, adding that they may have been partly motivated by “the day out and perhaps the excitement of a day’s action”.
He accepted the defendants were not the organisers of the protest but said they were “willing volunteers”.
The judge said the court “accepts a conscientious motive may be a relevant consideration” but that “your actions were disproportionate to your aims”.
He added: “You are all intelligent people and more than capable of working out why you’re in this position and what you need to do to avoid it.”
The defendants were all either retired, students or recent graduates at the time of the protest, the court was told.
Simonsen smiled and waved to the public gallery as he was led to the cells, while Higginson shouted — referring to details mentioned earlier in the proceedings — that her “vegan diet did not make me ill”.
There were gasps at the start of the judge’s sentencing when he told the six defendants: “In all but the case of Daniel Johnson those [sentences] will be for immediate terms of imprisonment.”
They sought to cause maximum disruption in an effort to force the government into a ban on new fossil fuel exploration in the North Sea,a demand that has become policy under the new Labour government.

https://www.thetimes.com/world/us-world/.title: Starbucks CEO in hot water over 1,000-mile commute by private jet
https://www.thetimes.com/world/us-world/.subtitle: Brian Niccol will travel from California to Seattle. Greenpeace have already criticised it as an ‘unjustifiable perk’
https://www.thetimes.com/world/us-world/.text:
When three twentysomething graduates named their new Seattle coffee venture after Starbuck, the steadfast first mate in Moby Dick, they could hardly have guessed that its future boss would gain notoriety for an epic voyage of his own — to the office.
Starbucks revealed this week that its new chief executive would not only be commuting the 1,000 miles from his home in Newport, California, to the company’s headquarters in Seattle, but he would be doing so by private jet.
When Brian Niccol, 50, joins next month he will not have to relocate to the state of Washington, where 4,000 Starbucks staff are based, but will instead be allowed to join the millions of Americans now enjoying “work from home” privileges.
The commute seemed to critics incompatible with the company’s 2020 pledge to reduce its carbon emissions by half over the next decade.
A Starbucks representative told CNBC that Niccol, who helped revive the Mexican food chain Chipotle after a series of poisoning incidents, will be expected to work from the Seattle office at least three days a week, in line with its hybrid work policies.
“Brian’s primary office and a majority of his time will be spent in our Seattle Support Center or out visiting customers and employees in our stores, and offices around the world,” the spokesman told The Times.
The business will set up a small remote office in Newport Beach for Niccol to use when working from California. He is also believed to have successfully negotiated a similar deal with his previous company.
“Going to need a lot more paper straws for this one,” joked one user on X, a reference to Starbucks’ introduction of sustainable straws to reduce landfill waste.
“If this man is commuting regularly on a private jet, do not let @Starbucks convince you they are environmentally conscious,” wrote another.
Others were more forgiving, pointing out the warmer climate in California was more favourable than the wetter Seattle weather. One X user wrote: “It’s jammy, but if you can swing it, why would you not?!”
Environmental scientists and climate activists were critical, however.
“As the world faces unprecedented heat waves, droughts, floods and other dire consequences of an accelerating climate crisis, it is unjustifiable for companies to offer company aircraft as employee perks,” Clara Thompson, a campaigner at Greenpeace, said.
“These jets are a stark symbol of social and climate injustice, where a privileged few indulge in the most environmentally damaging form of travel for mere convenience.”
According to the terms of his offer, Niccol’s annual base pay will be $1.6 million. On top of that he could get a performance-related bonus of as much as $7.2 million, and up to $23 million a year in Starbucks shares.
The announcement came as the coffee chain looks to boost flagging sales.
Niccol began his career in brand management at Procter and Gamble. He rose to executive level at Pizza Hut and later Taco Bell before leaving to join Chipotle in 2018. While in the role, the fast food chain’s sales doubled and its shares surged from less than $7 each to more than $50. His net worth is estimated at $60 million.
• Starbucks ousts Laxman Narasimhan as chief executive
In a 2019 interview, he spoke about the importance of a work-life balance and revealed how much he valued the time he spent with his wife, Jennifer, and their three children.
Most companies still prefer their executives to maintain a primary residence near their headquarters, though there have been notable exceptions.
Victoria’s Secret has made a concession in allowing its new chief executive, Hillary Super, to be based at the retailer’s New York City offices, rather than at the company’s headquarters near Columbus, Ohio. David Calhoun, who headed up Boeing, started working from home when he took over before the pandemic and never relocated close to its main base in Arlington, Virginia.
Dan Coatsworth, an investment analyst at AJ Bell, said using a private jet would also send a bad message to customers and staff, and would not be a “practical way to run a $105 billion business” with about 400,000 employees.
“A leader needs to be at the heart of a business,” he said, “not sitting on the beach enjoying the perks of the job.”
Andrew Trull, a Starbucks spokesman, said in an emailed statement on Thursday: “Brian’s schedule will meet or exceed the hybrid work guidelines and workplace expectations we have for all partners, which sees employees required to work from the Seattle office at least three times a week.”

https://www.thetimes.com/comment/letters.title: Just Stop Oil should target Glastonbury
https://www.thetimes.com/comment/letters.text:
In your sympathetic account of the caring family left behind by Louise Lancaster, the mother sentenced to four years for her part in the Just Stop Oil protests, it is said that she saw no choice but to disrupt the M25 (News Review, last week). Really?
She could have disrupted the woke faithful at Glastonbury, an appalling love-fest of financially privileged left-wingers hell-bent on polluting the countryside. Or targeted youthful backpackers, whose selfies from a brief bus ride in Thailand seem to imply we should forget about the long-haul flight to get there. Yes, climate change is serious. What many of us object to in Just Stop Oil’s approach is the hypocrisy in choice of targets.Sandra M Towers, Wigton, Cumbria
Caroline Scott’s report on the jailing of Louise Lancaster provides further evidence of disproportionate sentencing being handed down by judges. Four years for helping to organise a non-violent protest in which she did not take part was excessive. As her former husband says, the average sentence for violent crime is less than two years. In a healthy society the laws that the police have to enforce must have public respect. This is being eroded. The new justice secretary should put proportionality in sentencing at the top of her agenda.Robin Laurance, Oxford
Four years is the same sentence Steven van de Velde, the Dutch beach volleyball player, was given for child rape. He was sentenced in a UK court. I wonder if those who call for draconian punishments for Just Stop Oil protesters will make similar calls for tarring and feathering of farmers, next time their “go slow” protests disrupt traffic. Kieran Roberts, Glasgow

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/law/article/.title: Just Stop Oil activists appeal sentences after rioters given shorter terms
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/law/article/.subtitle: The five climate campaigners who were convicted for conspiring to block the M25 say their sentences were ‘manifestly excessive’ and breached international law
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/law/article/.text:
The five JSO activists who were convicted for conspiring to block the M25 have appealed against their record sentences, claiming the terms breached international law and are longer than those handed to rioters.
Roger Hallam, 58, was jailed for five years for co-ordinating the protests that disrupted the M25 in London over four days in 2022. Forty-five protesters climbed gantries on the motorway, forcing police to stop the traffic.
Daniel Shaw, 38, from Northampton, Lucia Whittaker De Abreu, 35, from Derby, Louise Lancaster, 58, from Cambridge, and Cressida Gethin, 22, from Hereford, were each sentenced to four years after being found guilty of conspiring to cause a public nuisance.
The group were sentenced under controversial legislation introduced by the previous government to get tougher on disruptive tactics used by environmental protesters, including blockading roads and attacks on sporting events. A 13-week campaign by Just Stop Oil (JSO) last summer cost the Metropolitan Police more than £7.7 million, the equivalent cost of 23,500 officer shifts.
The legislation, which provides stiffer sentences for protesters who block roads, was backed by Sir Keir Starmer, now the prime minister. However, it was condemned by the United Nations human rights commissioner as “deeply troubling” and “disproportionate”, with Dale Vince, a millionaire Labour Party donor, calling on Labour to intervene in the case.
The activists will argue that the sentences were “manifestly excessive” and that the judge “appears to have punished the defendants for disobeying his orders not to explain their motivations for taking such action”. They will also argue that they were barred from producing evidence of the immediate threat posed by climate change.
The Times also understands that campaign groups are planning a new wave of action calling for the release of climate activists from the UK’s prisons.
A spokesman for Defend Our Juries said: “Both the recent race riots and the filling of our prisons with climate truth-tellers result from the previous government’s attempt to distract from the existential crises we face by demonising easy targets. It’s time to leave that toxic legacy behind, and to bring people together with an honest confrontation with reality.”
A spokesman for Just Stop Oil claimed that “direct action works” and that it was only after the group disrupted the M25 that Starmer committed to ending licenses for new oil and gas.
“The Whole Truth Five [the five jailed JSO activists] along with others did the best thing they could, according to the evidence, to prevent catastrophic and irreversible harm to the public and life on earth,” the spokesman said.
“Judge Hehir’s imagined ‘deterrent effect’ is both cynical and naive: it assumes we don’t love our children, but we do. It assumes we have no care for the future of our country, but we do. It assumes we don’t want to live, but we do.”
The appeal also comes as Avaaz, an America-based campaign group, started a national petition condemning the “gagging and jailing of peaceful climate protesters in UK courts”.
The petition, which also calls on Starmer to repeal the “repressive” Tory legislation and “restore the UK’s influential role in upholding democratic rights and international law”, has so far gathered more than 20,000 signatures.
